name: Batching & KV caching
summary: Serving tricks that process many users at once and avoid recomputing work already done.

D1.guide: Guess first: is a bus or a line of cars quicker for fifty people?
text: A bus carries many people at once instead of one car per person. Batching sends many people's questions through the AI together.
The AI also keeps notes on what it has already read (a cache), so it doesn't re-read the whole conversation for every word.
D1.analogy: A bus instead of one car per person.

text: Each generation step reads the model's weights; putting many requests in one step shares that expensive read across users.
**Continuous batching** adds and removes requests at every step, so short requests don't wait for long ones.

The **KV cache** stores intermediate results for tokens already processed, so each new token only does its own share of the work. It grows with context length and number of users, and its memory becomes the limit.

loop.label: next step; requests join and leave

D2.analogy: A bus instead of one car per person.
D2.analogyBreaks: A bus waits for passengers to board. Continuous batching lets riders get on and off at every step, and each rider's luggage (their KV cache) takes space that limits how many fit.

predict.question: Why does serving throughput usually rise when more users are batched together?
options: Each read of the weights from memory is shared by more requests
The GPU runs at a higher clock speed
predict.explanation: Generation is often limited by memory reads; batching spreads each read over many requests until compute or KV-cache memory becomes the limit.

text: Each step of generation reads the model's weights once. If many users share that step, the expensive read is shared too, so the total output rises almost in step with the batch.
Each user still waits for the step, and each user's cache also has to be read. Slide the batch size and watch total speed and per-user speed separately.

interactiveConfig.note: Illustrative numbers, not measured. Generic model sizes and a made-up accelerator, not real products. Speeds are upper bounds from the formula: weights plus each user's KV cache read per step, against compute of 2 FLOPs per weight per user.

tasks: With 250 tokens per conversation, go from 1 to 32 users. How much does each user's speed drop?
Keep going to 256 users. What stops the total from rising?
Switch to 4,000 tokens per conversation. How many users fit before memory runs out?

predict.question: With short conversations, you go from 1 user to 32 users on the same chip. What happens to each user's speed?
predict.explanation: The weights are read once per step for everyone. Only the small per-user cache reads are added, so each user keeps most of their speed while the total rises about 30 times.

text: The **KV cache** stores a key and a value for every past token, in every layer, so the model does not recompute them. Its size is **2 × layers × KV heads × head size × bytes × tokens × users**.
The weights are a fixed cost. The cache grows with every token of context and every user, so on a busy server it soon overtakes the weights and becomes the memory budget.

interactiveConfig.note: Illustrative model shapes for generic 8B-class and 70B-class models, not real products. Sizes come from the formula; real servers add overheads.

tasks: With the 8B-class model, find a context length and user count where the cache is bigger than the weights.
Double the context, then double the users instead. Do they cost the same?
Switch the cache to 8-bit. How many more users fit in the same memory?
D4.code:
kv_per_token = 2 * layers * kv_heads * head_size * bytes   # a key and a value per layer
cache = kv_per_token * context_tokens * users
weights = params * weight_bits / 8
free = device_memory - weights
max_users = free // (kv_per_token * context_tokens)
tradeoffs: Longer contexts and more users both grow the cache in direct proportion.
Fewer KV heads (grouped-query attention) shrink the cache but change the model.
A lower-precision cache saves memory at some risk to accuracy.
Paging the cache in small blocks wastes less memory, and sharing common prefixes avoids storing the same tokens twice.

predict.question: For the 8B-class model with a 16-bit cache, about how many tokens in total, across all users, make the cache as big as the 16 GB of weights?
predict.explanation: Each token costs 2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 131,072 bytes. 16 GB ÷ 131,072 bytes is about 122,000 tokens: for example 8 users with 16,000 tokens each.

text: Frontier: paged KV-cache memory management, sharing cached prefixes across users, running the prompt-reading and generation phases on different machines, and compressing the KV cache for very long contexts.
